name: Felix Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cook at Noodle Yard, a ramen bar in a small university town, and on a term-time Saturday we do about two hundred bowls. I start at ten, check the broth that's been simmering overnight, boil eggs, slice pork belly, and portion noodles into little nests. During service I run the noodle station, ninety seconds a bowl, shouting times to Kemi on garnish. I love the speed and the students, but the pay is low and the steam fogs my glasses all day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI or tech in your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, honestly. I use an AI assistant to turn our sales numbers into a prep list, so I know how many eggs to marinate on a Thursday. On Sundays I sell dumplings at the farmers' market, and the AI helps me cost them and write the posts. I live with my boyfriend Arun, who drives buses, and between the rent and my van loan I've got about two hundred pounds saved, which isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit disappointing, actually, because I'd hoped it would take more of the boring stuff off us. At work I'd say the prep-list trick still works, so I'm keeping it. Online I'd say the real story is that the tech bosses oversold it and the money should've gone into public services.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my life stays the same, which is tight. Noodle Yard is busy in term time and dead in summer, when they cut me to three days. That's the real problem, the summer gap, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for my prep lists and the dumpling stall, because it saves me an hour a week. I'd try to grow the market stall so it covers the summer dip, maybe add a second market in the next town. And I'd keep pushing my mates at work to join the union, even if the ramen bar's tiny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels a bit flat, but okay. I'm used to living close to the edge, and I've got the stall to lean on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the dumpling stall actually bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a good Sunday about a hundred and twenty after costs, on a wet one maybe forty. Over summer it's what pays the electric. If I added the Wednesday market in Ashby, the next town over, I reckon I could double it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the summer gap like in real money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From June to September I lose two days a week at the ramen bar, so about four hundred a month. Arun covers more of the rent then, which I hate. We've argued about it twice, not badly, but it sits there.

say: I'd say it's **disappointing** that AI didn't take more boring work off us.
I'd say tech bosses **oversold** it and money should go to public services.
think: I think the real problem is the **summer gap**, when hours drop to three days.
I think life stays **tight**, with about two hundred pounds saved.
do: Keep using AI for **prep lists** and dumpling stall costing.
Add the **Wednesday market** in Ashby to double stall income.
Keep encouraging workmates to **join the union**.
feel: He feels **flat but okay**, used to living close to the edge.
S0.quote: From June to September I lose two days a week at the ramen bar, so about four hundred a month.
fieldNote: Felix is the rare cook who uses **AI daily** and wanted it to do more.
His **dumpling stall** is a real side income that cushions the summer.
Money tension with **Arun** over rent is a quiet, ongoing strain.

steps.text: Keep generating weekly prep lists with the AI assistant
Add a Wednesday dumpling stall at the Ashby market
Talk Noodle Yard workmates into joining the union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if workers get a share, and bad if they don't. At work I'd show people how I already use AI, so nobody's scared of it. Online I'd say the gains should go into shorter weeks and better pay, not just owners' pockets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in a decent spot, because the thinking bits of my work are already half done by AI. The risk is the broth and noodle side, because noodle machines and automatic boilers already exist. But that's slower, and I'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to set up the AI ordering and stock system for Noodle Yard, and ask for a bit more pay to run it. I'd grow the dumpling stall into online pre-orders, because AI handles the messages for me. And I'd do a free online course on food business basics, so I could run something myself one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting and a bit nervous, like the first day at a new kitchen. I think I'd come out of it okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask for more pay to run the system. Would the owner agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our owner Sandra is careful with money, but she's not stupid. If I show her it cuts food waste by even five percent, that pays for my raise. If she says no, I've at least learned something I can sell somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the kitchen would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kemi on garnish, because she hates phones and won't touch the tablet. And the kitchen porter, because dish machines are getting clever. I'd want to help Kemi learn, but you can't make someone want to.

say: I'd say AI is good only if **workers get a share** of the gains.
I'd say gains should fund **shorter weeks** and better pay.
think: I think I'm in a **decent spot** since AI already does my thinking tasks.
I think **noodle machines** are the slower risk, and I'd see them coming.
do: Set up the **AI stock system** at Noodle Yard for extra pay.
Grow the stall into **online pre-orders** handled by AI.
Take a free **food business** course online.
feel: He feels **excited** and a bit **nervous**, like a first day in a new kitchen.
S1.quote: Our owner Sandra is careful with money, but she's not stupid.
fieldNote: Felix wants to **run the systems** rather than be replaced by them.
He measures his pitch in **food waste savings**, a practical argument.
He worries about **Kemi**, but accepts he can't force her to adapt.

steps.text: Pitch an AI stock and ordering system to the owner
Take dumpling pre-orders online with AI handling messages
Complete a free online food business course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a universal basic income, and I'd say it loudly. At work I'd tell everyone that we need to plan together, not each person for themselves. Online I'd campaign for the AI companies to be taxed hard and the money shared out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's two sides for me. The thinking side of a restaurant goes in 2028, which honestly I'm half ready for. But I'm a hands-on cook on low pay, and by 2031 the robots can boil noodles better than me, and I've got two hundred pounds saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years going all in on the dumpling business, because handmade food from a person might still sell. I'd learn to use the robot kitchen kits, so if Noodle Yard buys one, I'm the one who runs it. And I'd try to talk Kemi and Sandra into turning Noodle Yard into a workers' co-op, so we'd own the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels scary and weirdly hopeful at the same time. I'd be anxious, but I wouldn't freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the gap between thinking AI and robots change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me three years where I'm still needed with my hands but the planning is free. That's when I'd build the stall up, using AI for all the admin. By the time robots come, I want to be selling something people choose because a person made it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A workers' co-op is a big idea. Would Sandra go for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not at first, she built the place. But if she's tired and the machines are expensive, selling part of it to us might suit her. I'd need to find the money, which is the hard bit, maybe a co-op loan scheme.

say: I'd call for a **universal basic income** and say it loudly.
I'd campaign to **tax AI companies** hard and share the money.
think: I think the restaurant's **thinking side** in 2028 is something I'm half ready for.
I think by **2031** robots out-cook me, and I've got two hundred saved.
do: Build the **dumpling business** in the two years before robots.
Learn to run **robot kitchen kits** at Noodle Yard.
Propose turning Noodle Yard into a **workers' co-op**.
feel: He feels **scared and hopeful** at once, anxious but not frozen.
S2.quote: By the time robots come, I want to be selling something people choose because a person made it.
fieldNote: Felix uses the **three-year gap** to build a handmade food business.
His **co-op** idea joins his progressive politics with his love of tech.
His **thin savings** are the one weak point in an otherwise bold plan.

steps.text: Expand the dumpling stall to three markets a week
Train on the robot noodle kit if Noodle Yard buys one
Propose a workers' co-op to Sandra and the staff
Campaign online for a universal basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste them arguing about whether it's real. At work I'd suggest Sandra lets me trial AI ordering now, while there's time to get it right. Online I'd push for training money for hospitality workers, because we always get forgotten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years suits me better than two. Thinking AI by 2031 and robots around 2034 means I've got about eight years cooking with my hands. That's long enough to turn the stall into a small shop, if I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd trial the AI ordering at Noodle Yard next year and ask for a small raise for running it. I'd save every pound the stall makes in summer toward a shared kitchen unit, maybe five hundred to start. And I'd do a part-time course on running a food business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels mostly hopeful, with a knot of worry about money underneath. I'd be uneasy rather than frightened, most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a knot of worry about money. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From never having more than a few hundred quid since I left college. Every plan I make has a thin bit, and that thin bit is cash. If the van breaks down, the whole dumpling thing stops for a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Arun about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my boyfriend Arun that the buses go before the kitchens, because self-driving buses are already being tested. So we'd both be planning. I'd say let's be the couple that started early, not the couple that waited.

say: I'd say there are **five years**, so stop arguing about whether it's real.
I'd push for **training money** for hospitality workers.
think: I think **five years** suits me better than two.
I think I have about **eight years** of hands-on cooking to build a shop.
do: Trial **AI ordering** at Noodle Yard next year for a raise.
Save summer stall money toward a **shared kitchen unit**.
feel: He feels **mostly hopeful**, with a knot of money worry underneath.
S3.quote: I'd tell my boyfriend Arun that the buses go before the kitchens, because self-driving buses are already being tested.
fieldNote: Felix sees Arun's **bus job** as more exposed than his own.
His **van** is a single point of failure for the whole side business.
He frames the plan as a **couple** starting early together.

steps.text: Trial AI ordering at Noodle Yard and ask for a raise
Save five hundred toward a shared kitchen unit
Enrol on a part-time food business course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's use it to build fair rules. At work I'd keep saying the same thing, learn the tools, don't fear them. Online I'd write about how hospitality could be shorter hours and better pay if we do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it feels like the best of the three for me. Robots around 2039 means I'm cooking until about forty, and by then I want my own place. The thinking AI in 2036 would actually help me run it, with ordering and books done for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking at Noodle Yard for now and grow the stall slowly. I'd use AI for everything on the admin side, as I already do. And in three or four years I'd try to open a tiny dumpling shop, maybe with a business loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good, mostly. Not calm, because money is still thin, but I'd feel like I was steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any risk in waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the risk is I get comfortable and do nothing for five years. I've seen older cooks get comfortable and always say next year, so I'd set myself a date. Mine would be a shop by thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a shop by thirty-two realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eight thousand pounds, or a start-up loan, and a year of steady stall sales. And Arun on board, because his wage would carry us while the shop gets going. I'd also want a mentor, someone who's done it.

say: I'd call ten years a **gift** for building fair rules.
I'd keep telling cooks to **learn the tools**, not fear them.
think: I think I can cook until about **forty** before robots arrive.
I think **thinking AI** in 2036 would help me run my own place.
do: Keep cooking at **Noodle Yard** while growing the stall slowly.
Open a **tiny dumpling shop** in three or four years.
Look for a **start-up loan** and a mentor.
feel: He feels **mostly good**, like he's steering, though money stays thin.
S4.quote: I've seen older cooks get comfortable and always say next year, so I'd set myself a date.
fieldNote: Felix sees AGI by 2036 as a **business chance**, not a threat.
He knows his biggest risk is **complacency**, and sets a deadline.
His plan relies on **Arun's wage**, a dependence he admits openly.

steps.text: Keep the noodle station at Noodle Yard for now
Open a small dumpling shop by age thirty-two
Apply for an eight-thousand-pound start-up loan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my savings are nothing and I'd need time to build the stall. What would help is a basic income or a training wage, so I could take the risk without losing the flat. Cheap start-up loans for small food businesses would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd want if machines did the boring bits. If machines did the boring bits, I'd want to cook less and share more, like teaching kids to make dumplings. Nobody talks about that side, only who loses.

headlineQuote: If machines did the boring bits, I'd want to cook less and share more, like teaching kids to make dumplings.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old noodle cook** at a busy ramen bar in a university town.
He uses **AI every day** for prep lists and to run a Sunday dumpling stall.
He lives with his boyfriend Arun, a bus driver, and has about **two hundred** saved.
He backs **basic income and co-ops**, and wants workers to own the machines.
His mood stays **uneasy to anxious**, because his plans run on thin money.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, since he'd lack time to grow the stall.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **basic income** or training wage, plus cheap **start-up loans**.
